topic: Why yawns are contagious, and why it isn't about oxygen

sources.title: Yawning (Robert R. Provine), American Scientist 93(6), Nov-Dec 2005
sources.note: Review of his own experiments by the researcher who ran them.

sources.title: Yawning: no effect of 3-5% CO2, 100% O2, and exercise (Provine, Tate & Geldmacher, Behav Neural Biol 1987): PubMed record

claims.text: People widely believe we yawn because of a shortage of oxygen or too much carbon dioxide; Provine calls it a legendary but unsupported factoid.
claims.quote: People widely believe that yawning is a response to a shortage of oxygen in the blood or brain, or an excess of carbon dioxide; These legendary but unsupported factoids are repeated so often that they have a life of their own; tested the commonly cited but previously untested hypothesis that yawning is facilitated by higher than normal levels of CO2 or lower than normal levels of O2

claims.text: Robert Provine and colleagues published the oxygen and carbon dioxide test in 1987, on college-age subjects.
claims.quote: Behav Neural Biol. 1987 Nov; Provine RR(1), Tate BC, Geldmacher LL; Using human college-age subjects

claims.text: Robert Provine was a professor of psychology at the University of Maryland, Baltimore County.
claims.quote: Robert R. Provine is professor of psychology at the University of Maryland, Baltimore County

claims.text: Breathing pure oxygen did not reduce yawning, and air with extra carbon dioxide did not increase it, although both made people breathe faster.
claims.quote: breathing neither pure O2 nor gases high in CO2 had a significant effect on yawning although both increased breathing rate; breathing 100-percent oxygen did not inhibit yawning; did not increase yawning, although subjects did dramatically increase their breathing rate

claims.text: In Provine's tests, 55 percent of people watching a five-minute video of yawns yawned, against 21 percent watching smiles.
claims.quote: exposing subjects to a five-minute series of 30 videotaped repetitions of a male adult yawning; Subjects were more than twice as likely to yawn while observing yawns (55 percent) as to yawn while viewing a comparable series of smiles (21 percent)

claims.text: 30 percent of people who read an article about yawning for five minutes yawned, against 11 percent who read about hiccups.
claims.quote: reading about yawning triggers yawns; 30 percent of subjects who read an article about yawning for 5 minutes reported yawning during this period, versus 11 percent of a control group who read an article about hiccuping

claims.text: Thinking about yawning evoked yawns in 88 percent of subjects within 30 minutes.
claims.quote: evoked yawns in 88 percent of subjects within 30 minutes
claims.note: Not used: one number too many for a 45 s script.

claims.text: Once a yawn starts it runs its course, about six seconds on average; there are no half-yawns and you cannot stifle one.
claims.quote: once started, a yawn progresses with the inevitability of a sneeze; The yawn runs its course over about six seconds on average; There are no half-yawns, an example of the; a reason why you cannot stifle a yawn

claims.text: Provine concluded yawning and breathing are controlled by separate mechanisms; yawning does not serve a primary breathing function.
claims.quote: yawning does not serve a primary respiratory function and that yawning and breathing are triggered by different internal states and are controlled by separate mechanisms

myths.myth: We yawn to get more oxygen (or to blow off carbon dioxide).
myths.truth: Breathing pure oxygen or air rich in CO2 didn't change how often people yawned (Provine et al. 1987).

open_questions: What yawning is for is still debated; the script does not claim a function.
